content: Lactobacillus fermentum is a Gram-positive bacterium belonging to the genus Lactobacillus. It is associated with active dental caries lesions and is commonly found in fermenting animal and plant materials, as well as in sourdough. Certain strains of Lactobacillus fermentum are considered probiotic, or friendly bacteria, in animals. At least one strain has been used to treat urogenital infections in women. Some strains previously classified as Lactobacillus fermentum, such as RC-14, have been reclassified as Lactobacillus reuteri. Commercialized probiotic strains of Lactobacillus fermentum include PCC and ME-3. Lactobacillus fermentum is utilized in various applications, including food and feed fermentation. Some strains exhibit natural resistance to specific antibiotics and chemotherapeutics, raising concerns about their potential role as vectors for transferring antibiotic resistance genes from the environment to humans or animals. This bacterium is also a normal inhabitant of the human intestinal tract, with some strains linked to cholesterol metabolism. A microorganism is classified as a probiotic if it meets specific criteria, such as being of human origin, non-pathogenic, resistant to intestinal passage, and beneficial to the immune system. Lactobacillus fermentum has been identified as a potential probiotic. Probiotic use in food aims to prevent and treat various health issues, including allergies, neoplastic growth, and inflammatory bowel disease. Recent research has focused on the influence of probiotics on host metabolic functions, particularly cholesterol metabolism. Lactobacillus species have demonstrated the ability to remove cholesterol in vitro through mechanisms such as assimilation, binding to cell surfaces, and incorporation into cellular membranes. Lactobacillus fermentum exhibits strong pH tolerance, surviving and growing in solutions with a pH of 3 for several hours. It also demonstrates good bile tolerance when incubated with 3 g/L of bile salts. These characteristics are significant for its consideration as a probiotic, as it must withstand the stresses of the digestive system. Lactobacillus fermentum has been shown to survive these conditions, supporting its potential as a probiotic. One of the ways Lactobacillus fermentum acts as a probiotic is by reducing cholesterol levels. Studies using cholesterol broths have shown that Lactobacillus fermentum strains exhibit the highest cholesterol removal. Mechanisms include cholesterol absorption, incorporation into bacterial cell membranes, and interference with bile salt recycling, which increases the demand for bile salts synthesized from cholesterol. The strain Lactobacillus fermentum ME-3, discovered in 1994 from human fecal samples, has been identified as an antimicrobial and antioxidative probiotic. ME-3 demonstrates tolerance to bile concentrations and pH drops, classifying it as a probiotic. It suppresses Gram-negative bacteria and, to a lesser extent, Enterococci and Staphylococcus aureus, benefiting the host. ME-3 produces antimicrobial compounds such as acetic, lactic, and succinic acids, as well as putrescine. Research on its antioxidant properties in soft cheese products revealed its ability to prevent spoilage. Consumption of ME-3 positively influenced gut microbiota, increasing beneficial Lactobacilli. Its properties suggest it can protect against food-derived infections and oxidative damage. Studies in mice treated with a combination of ofloxacin and ME-3 showed reduced liver and spleen granulomas caused by Salmonella typhimurium. Lactobacillus strains are generally considered safe due to their association with food and their role as normal inhabitants of the human microbiota. They exhibit low pathogenic potential. Safety studies on Lactobacillus fermentum in mice showed no adverse effects on blood biochemistry, body weight, feed intake, or clinical signs such as diarrhea. These findings support the safety of Lactobacillus fermentum for use in food. An important consideration for the safety of Lactobacillus fermentum is the presence of transferable antibiotic resistance genes. For it to be considered a probiotic, it must not contain such genes, as their transfer could reduce the efficacy of antibiotics. Lactobacillus fermentum was found to be resistant to amikacin and norfloxacin, which are considered intrinsic resistances. Other studies have reported similar resistance patterns in lactic acid bacteria (LABs). Lactobacillus fermentum has also been associated with heat resistance. It is one of the main organisms involved in the spoilage of tomato products. Research has shown that pectins in tomato juice protect bacterial cells from heat destruction. The breakdown of pectin by enzymatic action increases bacterial susceptibility to heat. However, heating inactivates natural pectolytic enzymes, allowing Lactobacillus fermentum to remain heat-resistant. Heat resistance is influenced by the medium in which the bacteria are cultured, with better media resulting in higher resistance. Studies have demonstrated that Lactobacillus fermentum exhibits antibiotic resistance to vancomycin and tetracycline. Research has also identified the presence of tetracycline and erythromycin resistance plasmids in certain strains. Despite its resistance to some antibiotics, Lactobacillus fermentum is sensitive to others, including gentamicin, cefazolin, penicillin, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, ampicillin, carbenicillin, erythromycin, amikacin, and chloramphenicol.
